Foundations: how creams, lotions and facial oils work

Learn the difference between water-free oils and water-based creams, what every ingredient in an emulsion does, and how to set up a clean, safe workspace before you heat a single drop. This module builds on simple butters and oils and takes you into proper emulsions.

If you already make whipped shea butter or body oils, you are making **anhydrous** products. Anhydrous simply means "without water". Creams and lotions are different. They are mostly water, held together with oil in a smooth, white mixture. That mixture is called an **emulsion**, and making one well is the main skill of this course.
A pump bottle of lotion
A lotion in a pump bottle is usually an emulsion: water and oil held together by an emulsifier.
Oil and water do not mix on their own

Pour some groundnut oil into a cup of water and stir. Within a minute the oil floats back to the top. To keep tiny droplets of oil spread evenly through water, you need an **emulsifier**. An emulsifier is an ingredient with one end that likes water and one end that likes oil, so it sits between the two and stops the droplets joining back together. In home and small-scale skincare, the most common emulsifiers are sold as **emulsifying waxes**, white pellets or flakes that you melt with the oils.

Most body lotions and face creams are **oil-in-water** emulsions. That means small oil droplets float inside a larger amount of water. This is why a good lotion feels light, sinks in quickly and does not leave the heavy, greasy layer that pure shea butter can leave in hot weather.

Why makers move from butters to creams
**Feel:** many customers in hot, humid cities like Lagos, Port Harcourt or Warri find a light lotion more comfortable than a solid butter.
**Spread:** a lotion spreads easily over large areas such as legs and arms, so a little goes a long way.
**Cost per jar:** water is cheap compared with shea butter or imported oils, but the savings are partly used up by the emulsifier, preservative, better packaging and testing.
**Face products:** facial skin often prefers lighter textures, so light creams and facial oils open a new range.
A cream is a step up in responsibility

A badly made butter usually just feels grainy. A badly made or unpreserved cream can grow germs that customers cannot see or smell and then rub onto their face. Treat every water-based product as a product that must be made cleanly, preserved properly and tested before anyone else uses it.

Every cream, from a big brand to a home kitchen, is built from the same few building blocks. Once you can recognise them, any recipe becomes easy to read, and you can spot a recipe that is missing something important.
A test tube with liquid
Each ingredient group in a cream has one clear job, just like each reagent in a laboratory test.
The water phase

This is the biggest part of a lotion. It usually contains **distilled water** plus a **humectant**, an ingredient that draws moisture to the skin. Vegetable glycerin is the most common humectant and is easy to find from cosmetic suppliers in Lagos, Abuja and online. Too much glycerin makes a cream sticky, so follow a tested recipe.

Use distilled water, not tap, borehole, sachet or bottled water. Making Skincare, a formulation teaching site, advises against tap, bottled or mineral water because the dissolved minerals and other content can shorten shelf life. Distilled or deionised water is sold by chemical shops and pharmacies, often for car batteries or laboratory use; buy a sealed bottle and check the label says distilled or deionised.
The oil phase

This holds your oils and butters and the emulsifying wax. Light oils such as sunflower, sweet almond or fractionated coconut oil give a thin, quick-absorbing feel. Butters such as shea or cocoa make a cream thicker and richer. In a lotion the oils are often around 10 to 25 percent of the total.
The emulsifying wax

Emulsifying wax (often shortened to e-wax) is a ready blend that does the emulsifying for you. Humblebee & Me, a respected formulation blog, describes three widely used ones: **Polawax**, **Emulsifying Wax NF**, and **Ritamulse SCG** (also sold as Emulsimulse). All three must be melted with the oils. Ordinary beeswax is **not** an emulsifier; it will not hold water and oil together for long, which is why beeswax and water recipes often separate.

How much? In Humblebee & Me's simple moisturising lotion, 3 percent Emulsifying Wax NF holds 10 percent oil. The same author writes that she usually uses 5 to 10 percent e-wax when the oils total about 25 percent. More oil needs more emulsifier. Always start from the supplier's recommended range for your exact wax.
The cool-down phase

Some ingredients are damaged by heat. The most important is the **preservative**. Many preservatives have a maximum temperature on their technical data sheet; for example, Humblebee & Me notes that Liquid Germall Plus tolerates heat only up to 50°C. So the preservative, and any essential oil or vitamin E, go in after the cream has cooled.

Common optional extras
**Fatty thickeners** such as cetyl alcohol or cetearyl alcohol: these are waxy, not drying like rubbing alcohol, and they add body to a cream.
**Antioxidants** such as vitamin E (tocopherol): slow the oils going rancid. They do not stop germs.
**Plant extracts or hydrosols** such as rose water: these count as part of the water phase and still need preserving.
**Fragrance or essential oils:** optional, used at low levels in the cool-down phase, and best left out of face products for sensitive skin.
Same name, different product

"Emulsifying wax" sold in open bags in markets may not say which product it is. Buy from a supplier who can tell you the exact name and INCI (ingredient) name, such as Cetearyl Alcohol and Polysorbate 60 for Emulsifying Wax NF, and give you a usage rate. If the seller cannot tell you what it is, you cannot write an honest label.

A quick way to judge any recipe you find on WhatsApp, YouTube or Instagram is to ask three questions. Does it contain water or a watery ingredient such as aloe juice or rose water? If yes, does it name a real emulsifier, not just beeswax? And does it name a broad-spectrum preservative with a percentage? If any answer is no, the recipe is not ready for you to make for other people, however beautiful the video looks.

Safety with heat, alcohol and electricity
Hot liquids and flammable alcohol

Isopropyl alcohol is highly flammable. Never spray it near a gas flame or a hot burner, and let it evaporate fully before you switch on heat. Melted wax and water at 75°C can cause serious burns: use oven gloves, keep handles turned inward, and keep children out of the kitchen. Never leave a pot on heat unattended.
Keep the stick blender cable and sockets away from the water bath. Unplug the blender before touching the blade.
Use a stable, flat surface. A tipping jug of hot oil is the most common accident.
If NEPA (grid) power goes off mid-batch, do not leave a gas cooker unattended while you sort out the generator.
If hot wax or oil touches skin, cool it under cool running water for 20 minutes and seek medical help for large or deep burns.
Storing ingredients

Keep oils, butters and the emulsifying wax in closed containers away from sun and heat; light and heat speed up rancidity. Keep the preservative tightly closed and note its opening date. Keep distilled water sealed and never pour unused water back into the bottle. Store everything off the floor, away from kitchen food and out of children's reach.
Choosing containers for creams

Every time a customer dips fingers into an open jar, she adds germs and sometimes water to the cream. A pump bottle, a squeeze tube or a jar used with a small spatula reduces this. For lotions, pumps are the usual choice. For thicker creams, jars are common, so include a spatula or print "use clean, dry fingers or a spatula" on the label. Buy containers new and sealed, wash and sanitise them anyway, and let them dry fully before filling, because water droplets left inside a jar are an easy place for mould to start.
Make one corner your production corner
If you share a kitchen, choose one shelf and one box for skincare tools only. Do not use them for food. This prevents cross-contamination in both directions and makes your hygiene routine faster.

This lesson walks you through the full method for an oil-in-water cream using an emulsifying wax. The method is the same whether you make 100 g to practise or 5 kg to sell. What changes with experience is your speed, not the steps.
A thermometer
Temperature control is the heart of emulsion making: hot enough to melt and combine, cool enough to protect the preservative.
Before you start

Sanitise your workspace as in Module 1. Print or write your formula with the gram weight of every ingredient. Weigh the water phase into one heat-resistant jug and the oil phase, including the emulsifying wax, into another. Weigh the preservative into a small clean cup and set it aside, covered.
The method step by step
**Weigh the water jug.** Write down the total weight of the jug plus the water phase. You will use this to replace water lost as steam.

**Heat both phases.** Stand both jugs in a water bath (a pot with a few centimetres of simmering water) or on a hotplate. Making Skincare advises heating the water phase to around 75°C and holding it at that temperature for 20 minutes. Heat the oil phase to roughly the same temperature until the wax is fully melted; the oil phase does not need the 20-minute hold.
**Top up the water.** After the hold, wipe the outside of the water jug dry, weigh it again and add back hot distilled water to reach the weight you wrote down.
**Combine.** With both phases at a similar temperature, pour the oil phase into the water phase. If one is much cooler, the wax can set into lumps.
**Blend.** Put the stick blender head fully under the surface, then blend in short bursts for about a minute. Keeping the head submerged stops air bubbles being whipped in.

**Blend, cool, blend.** Humblebee & Me recommends a blend-cool-blend cycle: blend about a minute, leave about ten minutes, blend again, and repeat as it thickens. Stir gently with a spatula between bursts.

**Cool-down phase.** When the cream has cooled to about 45°C (the point Making Skincare gives) and is below your preservative's maximum temperature, add the preservative and any other cool-down ingredients. Mix very well so it is spread through the whole batch.
**Fill and rest.** Fill sanitised containers, leave the lids slightly open until the cream reaches room temperature to avoid condensation, then close and label with the batch code.

Why heat and hold?

Emulsifying waxes must be fully melted to work. Heating both phases to a similar temperature lets the wax spread evenly before it begins to set. Holding the water phase at temperature for a while is a common practice taught by formulation schools to reduce the germs in the water before the product is preserved. It does not replace the preservative: it simply gives the preservative a cleaner start.

Professional formulators write every recipe as percentages, not cups or spoons. Percentages let you make 100 g today and 5 kg next month with exactly the same result. They also make it easy to check preservative and emulsifier levels against the supplier's recommended range.
A balance scale
Accurate weighing turns a percentage formula into a repeatable product.
The one formula you need

**Grams of an ingredient = batch size in grams × percentage ÷ 100.** Humblebee & Me gives the same method for preservatives: a 50 g batch with a 2.5% ingredient needs 50 × 2.5 ÷ 100 = 1.25 g. Always weigh, never measure skincare ingredients by volume, because oils, glycerin and water all have different weights for the same volume.

Facial oils are one of the simplest and most rewarding products to make well. There is no water, no emulsifier and no preservative. Instead, quality depends on choosing good oils, keeping them fresh and packaging them so light and air do less damage.
A single droplet
A facial oil is used a few drops at a time, so freshness and a good dropper bottle matter more than volume.
Facial oil or serum?

The word "serum" is used loosely in shops. Some serums are oil blends, often called oil serums. Others are water-based, made with aloe vera juice, hydrosols or water thickened into a gel. A water-based serum follows all the rules of a cream: it needs a broad-spectrum preservative, a stable pH and testing. In this lesson you make an oil serum, which is anhydrous.

Rancidity: the enemy of oils

Oils react with oxygen over time and go rancid. You notice a sharp, crayon-like or paint-like smell. Heat, light and air speed this up, and oils rich in delicate fatty acids, such as rosehip, change fastest. Rancid oils can irritate skin and customers will notice the smell.
Buy fresh oil in quantities you will use within a few months, and ask the supplier for the batch and best-before date.
Add an antioxidant such as vitamin E (tocopherol) at the rate your supplier recommends. It slows rancidity; it is not a preservative.
Fill amber or cobalt blue glass dropper bottles, filled close to the top to leave less air.

Quality and safety: preservatives, pH, stability, labels and NAFDAC

Choose and use a broad-spectrum preservative correctly, measure and adjust pH, and run simple stability checks that show whether your cream stays safe and unchanged. Then write an accurate ingredient list and understand the NAFDAC basics for selling creams.
Using a broad-spectrum preservative correctly and checking pH
Explain why a cream needs a broad-spectrum preservative
Read a preservative's data sheet for usage rate, pH range and heat limit
Measure the pH of a cream with a calibrated meter or strips
Adjust pH safely in small steps

Your cream is mostly water. Bacteria, yeasts and moulds can grow in that water, often without any sign you can see or smell at first. A **broad-spectrum preservative** is one that is designed to control all three groups. Humblebee & Me puts the rule simply: if you are making something that contains water, you need a broad-spectrum preservative. This lesson is about using one properly, because a preservative only works when it is chosen, dosed and kept within its pH range correctly.
A laboratory petri dish
Microbes grow quietly in water-based products, which is why preservative choice and pH are checked, not guessed.
What "broad-spectrum" means

Some ingredients only work against bacteria, others only against moulds. A broad-spectrum preservative, or a ready-made blend, covers bacteria, yeasts and moulds together. Humblebee & Me lists several widely used examples, including Liquid Germall Plus, Optiphen Plus, Phenonip, NeoDefend and a gluconolactone and sodium benzoate blend, and warns that each has different strengths and weaknesses, so you cannot simply swap one for another.
Read the technical data sheet
Buy your preservative from a supplier who gives a **technical data sheet (TDS)**. From it, copy four facts into your notebook:
**Usage rate:** for example, Liquid Germall Plus is used at 0.1 to 0.5% according to Humblebee & Me.
**pH range:** the pH at which it works. For Liquid Germall Plus the same source gives pH 3 to 8.
**Maximum temperature:** Liquid Germall Plus tolerates heat up to 50°C, so it goes into the cool-down phase.
**Restrictions:** any product types or skin areas it is not recommended for, and its INCI name for your label.
Not preservatives

Vitamin E, rosemary extract, grapefruit seed extract, honey, salt and essential oils do not replace a broad-spectrum preservative in a cream. If a seller calls one of these a "natural preservative" for lotions, ask for a data sheet and test results.
Why pH matters

pH measures how acidic or alkaline something is, on a scale where 7 is neutral, lower is acidic and higher is alkaline. Healthy skin is slightly acidic: a study by Lambers and colleagues in the International Journal of Cosmetic Science (2006) found natural skin surface pH is on average below 5. Many creams are made slightly acidic to suit skin, but the deciding rule for you is simpler: **the finished cream must sit inside your preservative's working pH range**, or the preservative may not protect it.
Measuring pH
Wait until the cream is at room temperature, usually the next day; pH readings change with temperature.
Calibrate a pH meter with buffer solutions (commonly pH 4 and pH 7) following its instructions. Strips are cheaper but less precise; choose narrow-range strips if you use them.
Put a small sample into a clean cup. Never dip the meter into the whole batch.
Record the reading on your batch sheet. Rinse the probe with distilled water and store it as the instructions say.
Adjusting pH in small steps
Measure a sample
Add a few drops
Mix thoroughly
Wait and re-measure
Record the result
Go round the cycle slowly; adding a lot at once can push pH far past your target.
Worked example: bringing a cream into range
For example, Toyin in Abeokuta makes a 500 g cream with a preservative whose data sheet says it works best below pH 5.5. Her next-day reading is 6.4.
She dissolves 5 g of citric acid in 5 g of distilled water to make a 50% solution in a small labelled bottle.
She adds 3 drops to the whole batch, stirs for two minutes and measures a fresh sample: 6.0.
She adds 3 more drops, stirs and measures again: 5.6.
She adds 2 drops, stirs and measures: 5.2, which is inside the preservative's range.
She writes on the batch sheet: "pH 6.4 adjusted to 5.2 with 8 drops of 50% citric acid solution".
Toyin's preservative can now work as designed, and next time she knows roughly how much acid a 500 g batch needs.
Handle acids carefully
Citric acid is a food-grade acid but can sting eyes and broken skin. Wear gloves, label the solution clearly and keep it away from children. Add acid in drops, never by pouring.
The limits of home checks

Correct dose and pH give your preservative its best chance, but they do not prove it works in your exact formula. The recognised proof is a **preservative efficacy test**, often called a challenge test, done by a laboratory: the lab adds known microbes to your product and checks that the preservative reduces them over several weeks. Before selling at scale, budget for laboratory testing; NAFDAC registration also requires a laboratory certificate of analysis, which you will meet in Lesson 3.3.

A cream can look perfect on day one and separate, change smell or grow mould weeks later. **Stability testing** means storing samples under different conditions and checking them regularly so you find these problems before your customers do.
A spiral calendar
Stability testing runs on a calendar: the same checks, on fixed dates, for every new formula.
A simple three-temperature test

Making Skincare describes a three-month stability test with samples kept at room temperature, in a fridge at about 4°C, and in a warm place at 40 to 45°C, checked at 2, 4, 8, 12 and 24 weeks. Heat speeds up most kinds of failure, so the warm sample often shows problems first. In Nigeria, room temperature itself is often warm, which makes this test especially useful.
Fill at least three small, sanitised, identical jars from the same batch and label each with the batch code and where it will be stored.
Keep one at room temperature away from direct sun, one in the fridge, and one in a warm place checked with your thermometer. Keep a fourth sealed jar untouched as a reference.
On each check date, look, smell, feel and measure pH, and write results in your log.
Compare every sample with the reference jar and with your day-one photo.

Batch records

A batch record is the story of one batch: what went in, how it was made and what came out. Give every batch a code, for example NC-2610-01 for Natural Cream, October 2026, batch 1. Print the code on every jar.

Worked example: two versions compared
For example, Uche in Aba tests two versions of her body cream, version 1.0 with 5% e-wax and version 1.1 with 6% e-wax, side by side for eight weeks.
Week 2: both look fine at room temperature. In the warm sample, version 1.0 has a thin oily line on top.
Week 4: version 1.0 warm sample has clearly separated. Version 1.1 is unchanged in all three places.

The warm sample revealed a weak emulsion in four weeks, saving Uche from selling a cream that would have separated in customers' bags.
Setting a cautious shelf life

Do not print a long expiry date you have not tested. If your samples have only been checked for 12 weeks, do not claim two years. A cautious approach is to set the shelf life no longer than the period your tests and any laboratory results support, and to add a "use within" period after opening, such as 6 months, shown with the open-jar symbol. Extend dates only when longer tests support it.
Facial oils need stability checks too

For a facial oil the main risk is rancidity, not germs. Keep one bottle at room temperature away from light and one in a warm place, and smell both against a fridge-stored reference every month. If the warm bottle starts to smell sharp or like crayons after two months, your blend may not last long on a hot shop shelf. You can then lower the share of the delicate oil, such as rosehip, raise the share of a stable one such as jojoba, or switch to smaller bottles that customers finish sooner.

Also test your packaging. Fill one pump bottle and one jar from the same batch and use them yourself daily for a month. Note whether the pump clogs, whether the jar lid seals, and whether the label smudges with oily fingers. Packaging faults cause as many customer complaints as formula faults.

A cream label has more to say than a butter label: more ingredients, a preservative, and often a use-by period after opening. Customers with sensitive skin read these lists closely. This lesson focuses on getting the ingredient list right for an emulsion and keeping dangerous ingredients out.
A person reviewing a document
An ingredient list is a document customers rely on, so every line must match what is really in the jar.
Writing the ingredient list

Use **INCI names**, the international standard names for cosmetic ingredients that suppliers print on their data sheets, and list ingredients in order of weight, largest first. A blend such as an emulsifying wax or a preservative is listed as its separate parts. Your supplier's data sheet gives these INCI names; if they cannot, find a supplier who can.
Worked example: the learning formula as an ingredient list
For example, Rukayat turns the Module 2 body cream (water 70.5%, sunflower oil 12%, shea 8%, Emulsifying Wax NF 6%, glycerin 3%, Liquid Germall Plus 0.5%) into a label.

Emulsifying Wax NF is listed by Humblebee & Me as Cetostearyl (Cetearyl) Alcohol and Polysorbate 60, so both names appear. She asks her supplier how the 6% splits between them to place each correctly.

Ingredients that must never go into your cream

Creams are the product most often used to hide harmful "toning" or "lightening" ingredients. Never add hydroquinone, mercury compounds, steroid creams, antibiotic or antifungal creams, crushed tablets or any medicine. These can cause serious harm, and adding them turns your product into an unregistered medicine. If a customer asks you to "add something strong", say no and explain that you make cosmetic moisturisers only.
Allergens and sensitivities
**Nut-derived oils** such as sweet almond or macadamia: state them clearly, for example "contains almond oil".
**Essential oils and fragrance:** common causes of skin reactions; keep them low or leave them out, especially in face products.

**Preservatives:** some customers avoid particular preservatives. Diazolidinyl urea, for example, is known as a formaldehyde-releasing preservative, so people with that sensitivity will check for it. Listing every preservative by name lets them choose.
**Patch test advice:** print "Patch test before first use. Stop use if irritation occurs."

Directions also protect customers. For a body lotion, for example: "Smooth onto clean skin as needed. For external use only. Avoid the eyes. Keep out of reach of children. Store below 30°C away from direct sunlight. Use within 6 months of opening." Only print a storage temperature or use-by period that your own stability tests support, and adjust the wording to your product.

Ingredient safety also includes the raw materials themselves. Buy from suppliers who give data sheets and batch numbers, store each material in its original labelled container, and never transfer a preservative or acid into an unmarked food bottle where someone could mistake it for something else. If a raw material arrives without a label, smells wrong or has passed its best-before date, do not use it.
Honest words for creams

Describe what a cosmetic cream really does: moisturises, softens, helps skin feel comfortable. Avoid claims to treat eczema, acne, stretch marks, dark spots or any condition. Be careful with "natural" and "preservative-free". A cream with Liquid Germall Plus is not preservative-free, and saying so would be false and unsafe. You can honestly write "made with shea butter and sunflower oil, preserved for your safety".

In Nigeria, cosmetics are regulated by NAFDAC. Its Guidelines for the Registration of Cosmetics Made in Nigeria require, among other documents, business registration (a CAC business name is accepted for micro and small enterprises), trademark evidence for the brand name, an inspection of the premises, label artwork that complies with the Cosmetics Labelling Regulations, and a laboratory certificate of analysis. NAFDAC also runs services for micro, small and medium enterprises. Read the current guideline on the NAFDAC website or visit the nearest NAFDAC office before you apply, as requirements and fees are updated.
Your records are your evidence

The batch records, stability logs, data sheets and pH readings you have been keeping are exactly the kind of evidence an inspector expects to see. Keep them in one folder per product from your first batch.

Creams look cheap to make because most of the jar is water. But emulsifying wax, preservative, better packaging, labels and laboratory tests add up quickly. About the prices in this lesson
All naira prices here are approximate examples for practice only. Prices vary by city, supplier and month. Use the prices on your own receipts.
Step 1: cost per gram

For each ingredient, divide what you paid by the grams you received. If 500 g of emulsifying wax cost ₦8,000, the cost per gram is 8,000 ÷ 500 = ₦16 per gram. For liquids sold by volume, weigh a full container on your scale once, or use roughly 0.9 g per ml for most plant oils. Then multiply each ingredient's cost per gram by the grams in your batch.
Worked example: costing five 50 g jars of body cream
For example, Rukayat costs the 265 g batch from Module 2 (five 50 g jars plus a loss allowance), using approximate prices from her receipts.

Step 2: price with a target margin

Two kinds of product
Water-free or water-based?
Cream or lotion
Must have a preservative
Heat, blend, cool carefully
If you make whipped shea butter or body oils, you make anhydrous products. Anhydrous means without water. A facial oil is like that. It needs no preservative, but the oils can go rancid.
Creams and lotions are mostly water, held together with oil. That smooth mixture is called an emulsion. The moment a product contains water, bacteria, yeast and mould can grow in it.
So a broad-spectrum preservative, one that works against all three, is not optional.
A bad butter just feels grainy
A bad cream can grow hidden germs
Customers rub it on their face
Make clean, preserve, then test
A badly made butter usually just feels grainy. But an unpreserved cream can grow germs that customers cannot see or smell.
And then they rub it onto their face. So treat every water-based product as one that must be made cleanly, preserved properly, and tested before anyone else uses it.
Inside an emulsion
The building blocks of a lotion
Water phase: distilled water, glycerin
Oil phase: oils and butters
Emulsifying wax, melted with the oils
Cool-down: preservative, added last

Every cream has the same building blocks. The water phase is the biggest part: distilled water, plus glycerin, which draws moisture to the skin. Never use tap, borehole, sachet or bottled water. Their minerals can shorten shelf life.
The oil phase holds your oils and butters. Light oils give a thin feel, butters make it richer.
The emulsifying wax holds oil and water together. Ordinary beeswax is not an emulsifier. Beeswax and water recipes often separate.
The cool-down phase holds the preservative, which goes in after cooling, because heat can damage it.

Step by step
Heat, hold, blend and cool
Preservative goes in at about 45°C, below its maximum temperature.
Weigh the water jug and write it down
Heat both phases to about 75°C
Hold water 20 minutes, then top up
Pour oil into water; blend, cool, blend
At about 45°C add preservative, then fill
Weigh the water phase and oil phase into two jugs. Write down the weight of the water jug with its water.
Heat both jugs in a water bath. The water phase goes to about 75 degrees, and the oil phase to the same, until the wax is fully melted.
Hold the water at that temperature for 20 minutes. Then dry the jug, weigh it again, and add back hot distilled water to replace what was lost as steam.
With both at a similar temperature, pour the oil into the water. Keep the blender head fully under the surface, and blend about a minute. Then rest about ten minutes, and blend again as it thickens.
When it cools to about 45 degrees, add the preservative and mix very well. Fill sanitised containers and leave the lids slightly open until it reaches room temperature.
Judge the texture after 24 hours, because creams keep thickening as they cool.

Batch formula
Grams = batch × percent ÷ 100
Never raise the preservative 'to be safe'. Stay in its range.
Five 50 g jars = 250 g batch
Preservative: 250 × 0.5 ÷ 100 = 1.25 g
Add up: 250.00 g. Check!
Write recipes in percentages, so any batch size comes out the same. For example, Rukayat in Ilorin wants five 50 g jars. That is a 250 g batch.
Her learning formula has 70.5 percent distilled water. 250 times 70.5 divided by 100 is 176.25 g.
Emulsifying wax at 6 percent is 15.00 g.
The preservative at 0.5 percent is 1.25 g. That is why you need a 0.01 g scale. Always weigh, never measure by spoon or cup.
Every line adds up to 250.00 g. Some cream always stays on the jug, so add a 5 to 10 percent allowance.
Too much preservative can irritate skin, and too little leaves it under-protected. Stay inside the published range.

Stable light base, like jojoba
Delicate oils like rosehip in smaller amounts

Preservatives, pH, stability tests and honest labels
Preservatives, pH, stability tests and honest labels.
This is the video for module three of Natural Skincare.
Safe before it is sold
Germs can grow unseen in water
A preservative needs the right pH
Problems show weeks later
Labels must tell the truth
Your cream is mostly water. Bacteria, yeasts and moulds can grow in it, often with no sign you can see or smell at first.
A broad-spectrum preservative controls all three, but only when it is dosed correctly and kept within its pH range.
A cream can look perfect on day one and separate weeks later. So you test before you sell, and you write labels that tell the truth.
Data sheet
Four facts from the data sheet
Usage rate: e.g. 0.1 to 0.5%
pH range: e.g. pH 3 to 8
Maximum temperature: e.g. 50°C
Restrictions and INCI name
Buy your preservative from a supplier who gives a technical data sheet. Copy four facts. First, the usage rate. Liquid Germall Plus, for example, is used at 0.1 to 0.5 percent.
Second, the pH range where it works. For Liquid Germall Plus, pH 3 to 8.
Third, the maximum temperature. Liquid Germall Plus tolerates heat up to 50 degrees, so it goes in at cool-down.
Fourth, any restrictions, and its INCI name for your label. Remember, vitamin E, honey, salt and essential oils do not replace a preservative in a cream.
Worked example
Toyin brings her cream into range
Add acid in drops, never by pouring. Re-measure every time.
Next-day reading: pH 6.4; target below 5.5
Make 50% citric acid: 5 g in 5 g water
3 drops, stir 2 minutes: pH 6.0
3 more drops: 5.6. 2 more: 5.2
Record: 8 drops took 6.4 to 5.2

Measure pH the next day, at room temperature, on a small sample, never by dipping into the whole batch. For example, Toyin in Abeokuta has a 500 g cream. Her preservative works best below pH 5.5, but her reading is 6.4.
She dissolves 5 g of citric acid in 5 g of distilled water, making a 50 percent solution in a labelled bottle.
She adds 3 drops, stirs for two minutes, and measures a fresh sample: 6.0.
3 more drops give 5.6. 2 more give 5.2, inside the range.
She writes it on the batch sheet, so next time she knows roughly how much a 500 g batch needs.
Citric acid can sting eyes and broken skin. Wear gloves, label the solution, and keep it away from children.
Stability testing
The three-temperature test
Any mould or sour smell: stop. Do not use or sell that batch.
Fill 4 identical jars from one batch
Room, fridge at about 4°C, warm 40 to 45°C
Keep the fourth sealed as reference
Check at 2, 4, 8, 12 and 24 weeks
Look, smell, feel and measure pH
Fill small, sanitised, identical jars from the same batch, and label each with the batch code.
Keep one at room temperature, one in a fridge at about 4 degrees, and one in a warm place at 40 to 45 degrees. Heat speeds up failure, so the warm jar often shows problems first.
Keep a fourth jar sealed and untouched, as your reference.
Check at 2, 4, 8, 12 and 24 weeks.

Each time, look for separation, smell for sourness, feel the thickness, and measure pH. For example, Uche in Aba saw her version with 5 percent e-wax separate in the warm jar by week 4, while 6 percent stayed unchanged.
If any sample shows mould, fuzzy spots or a sour smell, do not use or sell anything from that batch. And never print a shelf life longer than your tests support.
Never, ever
Keep harmful ingredients out
Never add hydroquinone or mercury compounds to any cream.
No steroid, antibiotic or antifungal creams, no crushed tablets. That makes an unregistered medicine.
Do not claim to treat eczema, acne or dark spots. A preserved cream is not preservative-free.
Creams are the product most often used to hide harmful toning ingredients. Never add hydroquinone or mercury compounds.
Never add steroid creams, antibiotic or antifungal creams, crushed tablets or any medicine. If a customer asks you to add something strong, say no. You make cosmetic moisturisers only.
And say only what is true. A cream moisturises and softens. It does not treat eczema, acne or dark spots. A cream with a preservative is not preservative-free.
Before you print
List ingredients by their INCI names, largest first, with every part of the emulsifying wax and preservative. Water becomes Aqua. Add the net weight, and a batch code on every jar.
Add dates, directions, and for external use only.
Name nut oils, fragrance and preservatives, and print patch test before first use. Add your name and address.
To sell, NAFDAC registration needs business registration, trademark evidence, a premises inspection, a compliant label and a lab certificate of analysis.
Key points
Remember
Water in it? Broad-spectrum preservative
Cream pH inside the preservative's range
Adjust pH in drops; re-measure
Test at three temperatures; record batches
No medicines, no false claims, INCI labels
To remember. Water means a broad-spectrum preservative, and the cream's pH must sit in its range. Adjust in drops.
Test at three temperatures and keep batch records. And never add medicines or make false claims.

Mostly water does not mean cheap

Guessing prices can lose money
Creams look cheap to make, because most of the jar is water. But emulsifying wax, preservative, packaging, labels, labour and laboratory tests add up quickly.

Many new makers copy other people's prices, and only later discover they lose money on every jar. The naira prices in this video are approximate examples for practice only. Use the prices on your own receipts.
Worked example
Rukayat costs five jars of cream
Price = cost ÷ (1 − margin)
Cost per gram: 8,000 ÷ 500 g = 16 a gram
Ingredients for the batch: 836
Jars 2,000, labels 500, gas 300, gloves 300
Labour 3,000; testing set-aside 750
Total 7,686 ÷ 5 = about 1,540 a jar
Start with cost per gram. Divide what you paid by the grams you received. If 500 g of emulsifying wax cost 8,000 naira, that is 16 naira a gram.
Rukayat multiplies every ingredient in her 265 g batch by its cost per gram. The ingredients total 836 naira.
Then five jars with lids at 400 each, 2,000. Labels, 500. Gas, 300, and gloves and alcohol, 300.
Her own labour, 2 hours at 1,500 an hour, is 3,000. And she sets aside 150 a jar towards laboratory tests, 750.
The batch total is 7,686 naira, so each jar costs about 1,540. The ingredients were only about 170 a jar. Pricing at 1,000 because it is mostly water would lose money.
For a 40 percent margin, divide the cost by 0.6. 1,540 divided by 0.6 is 2,567, which she rounds to 2,600 naira. Then she checks what similar creams sell for nearby.

Lower cost safely
Where to save, where never to
Safe savings
Buy jars and wax in bulk
Make larger batches
Count failed batches honestly
Never
Cut the preservative
Skip pH checks
Use tap water
If your price is far higher than others, look for safe savings. Buy jars and wax in bulk once your formula passes stability tests, and make larger batches so labour per jar falls.
And count failed batches. If one batch in ten is lost, that adds about 10 percent to your cost.
But never save money by cutting the preservative, skipping pH checks, or using tap water.
Selling safely
Protect customers and your money
Will it lighten my skin? No, it is a moisturiser. Not tested for babies, so not recommended.
Only from preserved, tested batches, in labelled pots. No fingers in display testers.
Check the money arrived in your bank or wallet app before handing over. Screenshots can be faked.

Answer questions honestly. If a customer asks whether it will lighten her skin, say no. It is a moisturiser that keeps skin soft. If you have not formulated or tested it for babies, say you cannot recommend it for them.
Give samples only from preserved, stability-tested batches, in sanitised, labelled pots. Never sell cream scooped into unlabelled nylon or reused containers.
Confirm each order in writing on WhatsApp. Then check the money has actually arrived in your Moniepoint, Opay or bank app before you hand over goods, because payment screenshots can be faked.
